[[File:NPosthumus.jpg|thumb|[[Nicolaas Wilhelmus Posthumus|Posthumus]], IISH founder and director (1937–1952)]]

The '''International Institute of Social History''' ('''IISH'''; {{langx|nl| Internationaal Instituut voor Sociale Geschiedenis}}, '''IISG''') is one of the largest [[archive]]s of labor and [[social history]] in the world. Located in [[Amsterdam]], its one million volumes and 5,445 [[special collections|archival collections]] include the papers of major figures and institutions in [[Radical leftism|radical leftist]] thought. The IISH was founded in 1935 by [[Nicolaas Posthumus]] as an independent scientific institute. It is part of the [[Royal Netherlands Academy of Arts and Sciences]].

== Collections ==

The International Institute of Social History specializes in international labor and social history, including that of the Netherlands. As of 2000, it holds one million volumes, 80,000 audiovisual items, 2,400 serials, three million digital files, and 30,000 linear feet of manuscripts across 5,445 collections. Among the latter are institutional collections from [[Amnesty International]], [[Confederación Nacional del Trabajo]] and [[Federación Anarquista Ibérica]], the [[European Trade Union Confederation]], [[Freedom Press]], [[Greenpeace International]], the [[International Confederation of Free Trade Unions]], Russian [[Socialist Revolutionary Party]], [[Socialist International]], and the personal papers of [[Emma Goldman]], [[Karl Marx]], [[Max Nettlau]], [[Lev Trotsky]], [[Karl Kautsky]], [[Ernest Mandel]], and [[Sylvia Pankhurst]].{{sfn|Kloosterman|2001|p=373}} The institute is the foremost [[Anarchist archives|repository of anarchist documents]] in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Avrich |first1=Paul |author-link=Paul Avrich |title=Review of The American as Anarchist: Reflections on Indigenous Radicalism |journal=[[The American Historical Review]] |volume=84 |issue=5 |pages=1467–1468 |date=1979 |doi=10.2307/1861661 |issn=0002-8762 |jstor=1861661 |url=https://muse.jhu.edu/book/67873/pdf }}</ref><ref name="Suriano2010">{{cite book|last=Suriano|first=Juan|title=Paradoxes of Utopia: Anarchist Culture and Politics in Buenos Aires, 1890-1910|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=1hswDwAAQBAJ&pg=PA299|year=2010|publisher=AK Press|isbn=978-1-84935-044-0|page=252}}</ref>

== History ==

[[Nicolaas Posthumus]], a socialist and first chair appointment in economic history in the Netherlands,{{sfn|Kloosterman|2001|p=373}} founded the International Institute of Social History in 1935.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Bergvelt|first1=Ellinoor|last2=Knegtmans|first2=Peter Jan|last3=Schilder|first3=Marian|title=Colourful professors: 375 years of portraiture in the collection of the Universiteit van Amsterdam|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=qcZfbSRUYjcC&pg=PA121|year=2007|publisher=Amsterdam UP|isbn=9789056294496|pages=120–21|chapter=Nicolaal Wilhelmus Posthumus (1880-1960)}}</ref> To examine how [[labour movement|labour relations]] develop over time, IISG collected archives from all over the world. During the first years Posthumus succeeded in obtaining many papers from anarchists ([[Mikhail Bakunin|Bakunin]] manuscripts), other [[socialism|socialist]] and [[social democracy|social democratic]] and [[Marxist]] movements from Germany and Russia.<ref>[https://iisg.nl/rebels/en/content/anarchism 'Anarchism', Website IISG]</ref>

Before the [[Germans invaded the Netherlands]] in May 1940, Posthumus was able to move the most valuable archives to London. During the war, most remaining IISG archives were transported to Nazi Germany between June 1942 and September 1944 by agents of the [[Reichsleiter Rosenberg Taskforce]] led by [[Eberhard Kautter]]. They were not destroyed, but stored for eventual inclusion in the [[Advanced School of the NSDAP]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Roth |first1=Karl Heinz |title=The International Institute of Social History as a Pawn of Nazi Social Research |journal=International Review of Social History |date=1989 |volume=34 Supplement |pages=19-20}}</ref> Most of the papers were rediscovered in Hannover in 1946, and some other parts were later found in archives in Moscow in 1991, and returned to Amsterdam.<ref>[http://socialhistory.org/en/about/history-iish History of IISG (more)]</ref>

In 1989 the International Institute of Social History moved to new premises: an old warehouse at the Cruquiusweg in the eastern part of Amsterdam. This building also housed the [[Press Museum]] but in 2017 that museum became a part of the Dutch Institute for Image and Sound (Nederlands Instituut voor Beeld en Geluid) in Hilversum.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://beeldengeluid.nl/organisatie/persmuseum-en-beeld-en-geluid-verder-als-een-organisatie|title=Persmuseum en Beeld en Geluid: Verder als één organisatie|date=27 July 2018|website=Beeld en Geluid|access-date=July 27, 2018|archive-date=April 23, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200423174807/https://beeldengeluid.nl/organisatie/persmuseum-en-beeld-en-geluid-verder-als-een-organisatie|url-status=dead}}</ref> 

IISG hosts part of the [[IHLIA LGBT Heritage]] collection (LGBT Archives).<ref>"A number of individual, organisational and thematic archives are accommodated in the International Institute of Social History (IISH) in Amsterdam." In: [https://ihlia.nl/en/collection/ Collection IHLIA, Archives]</ref>
